question: Why does Spider-Man keep worrying about his web-shooters running dry?
core_premise: Spider-Man runs out of web-fluid in the middle of patrol and starts thinking about redesigning his web-shooters so he won’t be caught helpless again.
viewer_payoff: He realizes the shooters need a warning system, because going dry leaves him stranded and walking home in the rain.
viewer_hook: What does Spider-Man decide to change after his webs run out on patrol?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans like the contrast between Spider-Man’s flashy swinging and the mundane, relatable problem that his signature power depends on a finite supply of web-fluid.
sample_answer_items: He literally runs out of web-fluid during patrol and has to walk home in a storm.
The story shows Peter thinking about adding a warning indicator to the shooters.
The payoff is the practical fix: he wants a way to avoid being stranded when the webs run out.

issue_evidence.quote: Having run out of web-fluid while on patrol, Spider-Man is reduced to walking home in the middle of a summer storm. As he bounds his way home on the rooftops, Spider-Man considers the idea of upgrading his web-shooters so they have a warning indicator to tell him when he is running out of web-fluid so this situation doesn't happen again.

question: How does Superman force Glenmorgan to confess his sabotage?
core_premise: Superman uses a blunt, physically risky stunt to force a businessman to confess to sabotaging the train system.
viewer_payoff: He makes the businessman believe he’s in mortal danger, then lands safely and gets the crime admitted.
viewer_hook: How does Superman turn a balcony stunt into a confession?
why_fans_ask_it: It’s a striking Superman move: he wins by combining intimidation, perfect control, and a very specific moral outcome instead of a simple punch-up.
sample_answer_items: He threatens to throw Glenmorgan off a tall balcony unless he confesses.
Superman then throws both of them off the balcony and lands safely.
The payoff is the confession: Glenmorgan admits he sabotaged the train system.

issue_evidence.quote: Superman takes a businessman named Glen Glenmorgan hostage and threatens to throw him down from the balcony of a tall building unless the businessman confesses to his crimes.
Superman uses his powers to land safely with Glenmorgan in hand, for whom the experience convinces him to confess to having sabotaged the train system.

question: Why is Captain America willing to be the one who pays the price against Galactus?
core_premise: Captain America accepts that the Ultimate Nullifier requires a fatal bearer and volunteers himself for the sacrifice if needed to stop Galactus.
viewer_payoff: He’s willing to die if that’s what it takes to activate the world-saving plan.
viewer_hook: Why does Captain America step forward for the weapon no one survives?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because it distills Captain America’s ethos into a hard choice: someone has to die to stop Galactus, and Cap is the first to volunteer.
sample_answer_items: The Ultimate Nullifier needs a wielder who will almost certainly die.
Captain America immediately offers himself up when that sacrifice is required.
The payoff is that the heroes actually use the weapon setup to stop Galactus, and Cap survives only with his shield left behind.

issue_evidence.quote: Back at the mansion, Reed Richards is explaining that their Ultimate Nullifier is complete however it needs someone to wield it and they will surely die. Captain America enters the room with the wounded Bucky and offers himself up, Iron Man and Thor offer themselves in sacrifice as well.

With an energy boost from the heroes below the Silver Surfer succeeds in absorbing energy and channeling it back into Galactus causing him to overload, destroying them both in the process. The only thing that survives the blast is Cap's shield which he reclaims.

question: Why can’t Hades make Wonder Woman marry him even after she says she loves him?
core_premise: Wonder Woman refuses Hades’ attempt to bind her with her own Lasso of Truth, but uses truth about love as the key to breaking his control.
viewer_payoff: She admits the feeling is real, but proves love is not the same as surrender or marriage.
viewer_hook: How does Wonder Woman tell the truth and still refuse Hades?
why_fans_ask_it: The tension is classic Wonder Woman: truth is mandatory, but the emotional outcome is more complicated than a simple yes-or-no answer.
sample_answer_items: Hades forces Diana to wrap the Lasso of Truth around her own neck as proof.
Diana confirms the truth of her feelings but still breaks free and refuses the wedding.
The payoff is that love and truth don’t equal obedience; she can love him and still reject him.

issue_evidence.quote: With her wedding to Hades soon to come, the ruler of Hell forces Wonder Woman to place her own Lasso of Truth around her neck to prove that she truly loves him. Even as she confirms that she does truly love him, she breaks free of her bonds and escapes, as she will not marry him, regardless of whether she loves him or not.
He threatens to kill her, and though she admits that one day, he might - it will not be without a fight.

question: Why do the Avengers decide they need to grow bigger?
core_premise: The Avengers are reframed as a bigger, global-and-interplanetary response to a world that has become too large for the old team size.
viewer_payoff: The scale of the crises jumps from Earth-level problems to Mars and beyond, forcing a larger team response.
viewer_hook: What makes the Avengers realize they have to get bigger?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask it because it explains the core pivot from a traditional team book to the expansive ‘Avengers World’ era.
sample_answer_items: The book shows Ex Nihilo terraforming Mars and sparking an interplanetary crisis.
Tony Stark says the world has changed and the team’s old scale is no longer enough.
The payoff is the new Avengers World idea: the team expands to meet bigger threats.

issue_evidence.quote: On Mars, Ex Nihilo begins to terraform Mars. He wants to make it have life. So he creates green plants on the red planet. And an intergalactic war is brewing because of him.

Stark says the world changed when Cap was found. He also says that the best ideas are the simplest ones. And that they now have a new idea: with problems escalating since Cyclops' turn to the dark side, they need to grow bigger.

question: What are distinct examples of Daredevil’s radar sense in action across original print issues?
core_premise: Daredevil’s radar sense is shown in different combat contexts: in one issue it is disrupted by chaff and still gives only a vague read on an incoming object, while in another it is used tactically to identify an opponent’s exact weak point and defeat him.
viewer_payoff: The question is answered with two concrete, issue-grounded demonstrations of the same ability family: one where the sense is hindered but still gives partial warning, and one where it is used to identify a vulnerable joint and break the opponent’s defense.
viewer_hook: One issue shows his radar sense getting jammed; the other turns it into a pinpoint finishing move.
why_fans_ask_it: Fans want to see how Daredevil’s signature nonvisual sense works in practice, especially the contrast between its limits under interference and its offensive precision in combat.
sample_answer_items: A threat-detection example where chaff disrupts Daredevil’s radar sense and leaves him with only a vague read on an incoming attack
A combat example where Daredevil uses radar sense to locate an opponent’s exact weak point and land a decisive strike

issue_evidence.quote: His pursuer shoots projectiles into the air that explode, raining down “chaff” that counteracts Daredevil’s radar sense. Fully blinded from his surroundings, Daredevil picks up the vague impression of an object coming towards him, but is unable to pinpoint Captain America’s shield as it flies at his head from behind.
Daredevil uses his radar sense to find the exact weakest point in Bruiser’s knee, then unleashes a strike that completely shatters the bone.

question: How does Spider-Man’s spider-sense work in modern print comics?
core_premise: Spider-Man’s own power guide spells out that his spider-sense is a distinct danger-warning ability, and the issue also explains the rest of his powers in concrete terms.
viewer_payoff: The issue states that his spider-sense warns him of danger, giving a direct description of the power’s function.
viewer_hook: What exact warning does Spider-Man’s spider-sense give him?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because spider-sense is one of Spider-Man’s most famous abilities, but comics often use it in vague ways. A source that plainly defines the power answers the recurring how-does-it-work question.
sample_answer_items: It is described as a danger-warning sense.
The issue pairs it with his proportionate strength and webbing notes as part of the same power breakdown.
The payoff is a plain explanation of what the sense does, not just that he has it.

issue_evidence.quote: Peter also finds graphs that show the levels of his strength. With the proportionate strength of a spider Peter is able to lift hundreds of times his body weight. He also gained a “spider sense” that warned him of danger.

question: How does Superman’s solar flare ability change what he can do in modern comics?
core_premise: Superman’s modern status quo includes a dangerous new energy-release limit: he can fly again, but the solar flare that restored him also depleted him and made the power feel risky.
viewer_payoff: The issue explains that the flare destroyed his suit, drained his strength, and is considered dangerous, so the cost is built into the power itself.
viewer_hook: Why is Superman worried about using his solar flare again?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask because this is a major change to Superman’s classic power set. The curiosity is not just that he has a new attack, but what the catch is and why it feels risky.
sample_answer_items: It is described as a new ability that releases solar energy.
Using it destroyed his old suit and depleted his strength.
The payoff is the concrete cost: the power works, but it leaves him vulnerable and worried about using it again.

issue_evidence.quote: only he’s lost his powers for the time being, and he’s had to get a new suit. His ability to release a flare of solar energy had destroyed the old one and depleted his strength. and though he expects to recharge soon, he worries that the new ability is dangerous.

question: What are the secrets of Captain America’s shield in modern comics?
core_premise: Captain America’s shield is treated as more than a symbol: a later issue explicitly calls the story about revealing its secrets while Steve races around the globe after something he cannot even see.
viewer_payoff: The issue says the story is about revealing the shield’s secrets, and Steve’s globe-spanning pursuit is the mechanism that delivers that mystery.
viewer_hook: Why is Captain America chasing something he can’t even see?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because the shield is Captain America’s defining object, yet comics occasionally turn it into a mystery with hidden rules or properties. That makes a ‘what is the shield really?’ question evergreen.
sample_answer_items: The issue frames the shield as having secrets worth revealing.
Steve is racing around the globe after something he cannot even see, implying the shield’s mystery drives the plot.
The payoff is the promise of an actual answer about the shield, not just another fight scene.

issue_evidence.quote: Revealed: The secrets of CAPTAIN AMERICA’s shield! In this first installment of a two-part tale, the answers will be laid bare, as the super soldier must race around the globe in pursuit of something he can’t even see!

question: Why does Wonder Woman break Amazon law to save a mortal?
core_premise: Wonder Woman’s defining moral tension is that she will break her own rules to save someone, even when Amazon law makes the choice personally costly.
viewer_payoff: She risks exile from Amazon society after breaking Amazon law to save the person in danger.
viewer_hook: What does Wonder Woman risk when she saves the mortal?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask because Wonder Woman is often defined by the clash between duty, law, and compassion. The interesting part is the cost of her mercy, not just that she is heroic.
sample_answer_items: She gives up glory and risks exile.
The source makes the motive clear: saving a mere mortal matters more than personal advancement.
The payoff is the exact cost of the choice, not a generic lesson about heroism.

issue_evidence.quote: Diana longs to prove herself to her legendary warrior sisters. But when the opportunity finally comes, she throws away her chance at glory and breaks Amazon law, risking exile, to save a mere mortal.

question: What is the real source of Wakanda’s power in Black Panther’s modern comics?
core_premise: Black Panther’s modern Wakanda stories hinge on the idea that the nation’s real power is not only royal technology or the throne, but the people themselves.
viewer_payoff: He comes to see that the people themselves have their own secrets, mysteries, and power apart from the monarchy.
viewer_hook: What power does T’Challa realize Wakanda’s people have?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because this is a core Wakanda idea: is the country defined by its king or by its people? The story makes that tension explicit and answerable.
sample_answer_items: The monarchy has long reflected Wakanda’s will, but the story stresses that the people themselves possess power.
T’Challa realizes he underestimated the citizens’ secrets and influence.
The payoff is a concrete shift in where Wakanda’s strength comes from: not just the throne, but the populace.

issue_evidence.quote: The indomitable will of Wakanda—the famed African nation known for its vast wealth, advanced technology, and warrior traditions—has long been reflected in the will of its monarchs, the Black Panthers.
I wish he’d warned me that they, too, have secrets. They, too, hold mysteries. They, too, possess a power all their own.

question: How does Thor’s worthiness limitation on Mjolnir work in modern print comics?
core_premise: Thor is one of the few heroes whose defining weapon is also a strict test of worthiness, and modern print stories keep using that as a concrete limitation rather than a guarantee of access.
viewer_payoff: The issue states that Thor tries and fails to lift Mjolnir, proving that access depends on worthiness, not raw power.
viewer_hook: The hammer’s rule is stricter than Thor’s strength.
why_fans_ask_it: Fans want the exact rule behind Thor’s most iconic weapon and the surprising fact that strength alone is not enough.
sample_answer_items: He can be physically strong and still fail to lift it if he is not worthy.
The issue shows the limitation as absolute in the scene, not symbolic.
The concrete outcome is that he has to rely on another weapon instead.

issue_evidence.quote: In the year 893 AD, inside the great weapons hall of Asgard, Thor attempts to lift Mjolnir but is unable to do so.

question: Why does Batman refuse to let a young enemy be killed when the conflict turns brutal?
core_premise: Batman’s no-kill code is most revealing when a story pushes him toward executing or abandoning it and he instead chooses mercy or restraint with a specific consequence.
viewer_payoff: Batman states that Bao is only a traumatized seventeen-year-old and insists he needs help, not death, firmly rejecting the kill-or-discard logic of the conflict.
viewer_hook: Batman’s answer is about saving a damaged kid, not winning the fight.
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask this because Batman’s code is one of his defining traits, and stories often test whether he will still apply it under extreme pressure.
sample_answer_items: He judges the kid as someone shaped by trauma rather than someone beyond saving.
He explicitly rejects Ghost-Maker’s harsher solution.
The concrete resolution is that the boy should be helped instead of killed.

issue_evidence.quote: Bruce tells him that Bao's just a seventeen-years-old kid who five years before saw his parents killed by the Joker. He does not need to be killed, but to be helped.

question: What are distinct examples of the Speed Force being used to move through time, repair damage, or pay a cost in modern Flash comics?
core_premise: The Flash’s Speed Force stories often show time travel as a costly, destabilizing action: each attempt to fix the past can deepen the rupture and force a sacrifice.
viewer_payoff: One issue shows Barry trying to undo time-loss by running backward to fix his mistakes, and another shows the repair plan demanding a literal sacrifice to seal the rupture.
viewer_hook: Both examples turn Speed Force power into a repair job with a dangerous price.
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask this because Speed Force abilities are central to the Flash, but the exact tradeoff between speed, time, and consequence changes from story to story.
sample_answer_items: In The Flash #31 (2014), Barry runs back in time because the more he runs, the more he loses, and he is trying to fix mistakes caused by being too late.
In The Flash #35 (2014), future Barry says the Speed Force rupture must be closed by sacrificing the present-day Barry’s life to fill the hole with his energy.

issue_evidence.quote: The more he runs, the more he loses. So I'm running back. I'm running back to fix it all.
His plan for repairing it, though, involves sacrificing the present day Barry Allen to fill the hole with his Speed Force energy.

question: How does Kryptonite weaken Superman even after he stops the immediate threat?
core_premise: A trace amount of Green Kryptonite can temporarily strip Superman down enough to crash his mission and leave him vulnerable, even after he destroys the threat he was chasing.
viewer_payoff: You learn that even a small amount of Kryptonite can briefly drain Superman’s power after victory, forcing a crash landing before he can get back to Earth.
viewer_hook: Why does stopping the comet still leave Superman powerless for a moment?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because Superman is famous for near-invulnerability, so a tiny Kryptonite exposure that still swings the fight is a classic, counterintuitive limit.
sample_answer_items: Trace Green Kryptonite from the destroyed comet temporarily weakens Superman.
The weakening is enough to make him crash on an alien planet.
He then has to recover and fly back toward Earth after the interruption.

issue_evidence.quote: Superman flies through space to take care of a dangerous comet on a collision course towards Earth. He destroys the comet, but trace amounts of Green Kryptonite are present and temporarily weakens Superman's powers. He crash lands on an alien planet and levels a civilian construct.

question: Why does Daredevil put the costume back on after everything he has been through?
core_premise: Matt Murdock comes back to vigilantism because he decides the Devil has to be visible again after his recent trauma, even though he is badly out of shape and not fully recovered.
viewer_payoff: You learn that Daredevil returns because he wants criminals to know he is back, despite his fear and physical weakness.
viewer_hook: What makes Matt suit up again when he is still hurting?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask it because Daredevil’s toughest battles are often moral and psychological, not just physical: why keep fighting when the pain and guilt are still fresh?
sample_answer_items: Matt feels his radar sense has become another cage after the truck accident and his recent trauma.
He decides Hell's Kitchen needs to know the Devil is back and watching.
He goes out even though he is not fully in fighting shape.

issue_evidence.quote: Back in his apartment, now alone, Matt can't sleep. He thinks about how his radar sense now feels like another cage, just like the one that kept him from being Daredevil after the truck hit him. So, he decides to put on his costume and swing around Hell's Kitchen to remind anyone that intends to do bad deeds that the Devil is back and watching.

question: What does Wonder Woman’s showdown with Hades reveal about love and the Lasso of Truth?
core_premise: Hades tries to force Diana to prove love with the Lasso of Truth, but the real rule is that love cannot be coerced and Hades must first be able to love himself.
viewer_payoff: You learn that the lasso can confirm Diana’s feelings, but it cannot turn truth into consent, and Hades’ own self-love is the missing piece.
viewer_hook: Why does telling the truth still not let Hades control Diana?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because this turns a famous magical truth device into a debate about consent, genuine emotion, and whether love can ever be compelled.
sample_answer_items: Hades tries to make Diana prove her love by using the Lasso of Truth against her.
Diana says she truly does love him, but still refuses to marry him and escapes.
The story makes clear that Hades cannot force love without loving himself first.

issue_evidence.quote: With her wedding to Hades soon to come, the ruler of Hell forces Wonder Woman to place her own Lasso of Truth around her neck to prove that she truly loves him. Even as she confirms that she does truly love him, she breaks free of her bonds and escapes, as she will not marry him, regardless of whether she loves him or not.

question: How does the Negative Speed Force change the way Flash’s powers work?
core_premise: Barry Allen’s Negative Speed Force makes his powers volatile and harmful; instead of simply being faster, he risks causing collateral damage and has to fight his own anger to use it safely.
viewer_payoff: You learn that the Negative Speed Force is not just a boost; it makes Barry’s speed unstable, damaging, and physically punishing to use.
viewer_hook: Why does Barry’s speed start hurting the city instead of helping it?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans ask because the Flash’s core fantasy is effortless speed, and this storyline flips that into a dangerous power with a real cost.
sample_answer_items: Barry gains the Negative Speed Force after fighting Eobard Thawne.
Using it can cause real collateral damage, like tearing up a city street.
Even after a win, Barry is left bruised and in pain instead of instantly healed.

issue_evidence.quote: Following his acquisition of the dangerous Negative Speed Force while fighting Eobard Thawne, Flash struggles to use his powers. He accidentally causes vast damage to a city street and lets the Reapers escape, leaving him to wonder if his powers are causing more harm than good.

Earlier in the day Barry narrowly won a fight with Shrapnel by using a new aspect of his Negative Speed Force powers. Now Barry nurses his bruises and aches, which his super-speed metabolism would ordinarily have healed by now.

question: What is the Intergalactic Empire of Wakanda, and why does it change T’Challa’s world?
core_premise: T’Challa discovers that Wakanda is not just a nation but the center of an intergalactic empire bearing his name, which reframes his entire sense of home and rule.
viewer_payoff: You learn that Wakanda’s identity expands into a multiverse-spanning empire, completely changing the scale of T’Challa’s world.
viewer_hook: How can Wakanda be bigger than the kingdom T’Challa knows?
why_fans_ask_it: Fans care because it takes a familiar, grounded kingdom and turns it into a cosmic mystery with a bigger political and personal meaning.
sample_answer_items: Wakanda turns out to be part of a much larger intergalactic empire.
That empire exists across the multiverse and is founded in T’Challa’s name.
The revelation forces T’Challa to rethink what Wakanda actually is.

issue_evidence.quote: Now, he will discover that Wakanda is much bigger than he ever dreamed… Across the vast Multiverse lies an empire founded in T’Challa’s name. Readers caught a glimpse of it in MARVEL LEGACY #1. Now find out the truth behind the Intergalactic Empire of Wakanda!

question: How does Superman’s solar flare work?
core_premise: Superman’s hidden solar-flare ability is not just a burst of power; it also drains his stored solar energy completely, leaving him powerless until he recharges.
viewer_payoff: The flare is a last-resort burst that converts all stored solar energy into one explosive attack, but the cost is total power loss until he recharges.
viewer_hook: The move strips him down to nothing and wipes out his powers in one shot.
why_fans_ask_it: It explains a dramatic late-era Superman power that looks overwhelming but has a surprising built-in downside.
sample_answer_items: It releases the energy stored in every cell at once
It burns off his uniform/armor and leaves him powerless
He has to recharge before flight and other powers return

issue_evidence.quote: In the safety of the Khentii Mountains in Outer Mongolia, Superman tests his new ability, a powerful solar flare. The heat burns away his uniform, and when Batman arrives in his Batplane offering a ride, he must board it naked - and powerless.

He can, in fact, unleash the energy stored in every cell in his body - resulting in a powerful solar flare. The blast burnt off his Kryptonian armour, and depleted all of his solar energy. His power of flight will be gone until he recharges.

question: What are distinct examples of Spider-Man’s webbing as a combat and problem-solving tool?
core_premise: Spider-Man’s webbing is a flexible toolset, and different issues show it being used for very different combat outcomes, from restraint to escape and anti-theft tactics.
viewer_payoff: The examples show that webbing is not one trick but a versatile combat and cleanup tool with very different on-page uses.
viewer_hook: One issue shows webbing as a quick arrest tool; another shows him having to melt it off when it sticks too well.
why_fans_ask_it: Readers like seeing how Spider-Man’s signature power changes from scene to scene and solves problems in unexpected ways.
sample_answer_items: He restrains Copperhead quickly and quietly with webbing
He uses acetone to melt webbing when it sticks in a fight
He can use webbing to control the pace and outcome of a confrontation

issue_evidence.quote: As Anti-Venom leaves, Spidey snatches a bottle of acetone to melt the webbing.
After quickly and quietly restraining him with webbing, one of the bankers as well as Copperhead notice that he was in a hurry.
